title: Drug Interaction Report – Patient A
content: Patient A is a 67-year-old male prescribed Warfarin (5 mg/day) and Aspirin (100 mg/day) following a deep vein thrombosis event in March 2024. Concomitant use of these two agents significantly increases bleeding risk due to their complementary anticoagulant mechanisms. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), while Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet aggregation via COX-1 inhibition. The clinical team recommends monitoring INR weekly for the first month, then biweekly once stable. Target INR range is 2.0–3.0. Any INR above 3.5 should trigger a dose reduction review. Patient A has a documented history of mild renal impairment (eGFR 58 mL/min), which slows Warfarin clearance and increases sensitivity. Dietary intake of vitamin K (leafy greens, broccoli) should remain consistent, as fluctuations directly affect INR. Concomitant NSAIDs, antibiotics (especially fluoroquinolones and metronidazole), and proton pump inhibitors may further elevate INR and require additional monitoring.

title: Side Effects Summary – Metformin
content: Metformin (biguanide class) is the first-line oral antidiabetic drug recommended by most major diabetes guidelines for Type 2 diabetes management. It works primarily by reducing hepatic glucose production and improving peripheral insulin sensitivity. Common side effects are predominantly gastrointestinal and include nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, flatulence, and abdominal discomfort. These effects are typically dose-dependent and often improve after the first 4–6 weeks of therapy. To minimise GI intolerance, Metformin should be taken with or immediately after meals and doses should be titrated gradually. The standard starting dose is 500 mg twice daily or 850 mg once daily, increasing by 500 mg per week up to a maximum of 2000–2500 mg/day. Lactic acidosis is a rare but potentially fatal adverse effect occurring at an estimated rate of 3 cases per 100,000 patient-years. Risk is elevated in patients with renal impairment (contraindicated if eGFR < 30), hepatic disease, excessive alcohol use, or acute illness causing dehydration. Metformin should be temporarily withheld 48 hours before and after administration of iodinated contrast agents. Vitamin B12 deficiency may develop with long-term use due to impaired absorption in the terminal ileum; annual monitoring of B12 levels is recommended for patients on Metformin for more than 3 years.

title: Clinical Trial Summary – NovaDrug X
content: NovaDrug X is an investigational GLP-1 receptor agonist developed for the treatment of Type 2 diabetes and obesity. The Phase II randomised controlled trial enrolled 240 participants across 12 sites in Germany, Spain, and the Netherlands. Inclusion criteria: adults aged 30–75, BMI ≥ 27, HbA1c between 7.5% and 10.5%, on stable background therapy for at least 3 months. Exclusion criteria included eGFR < 45, personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, and active pancreatitis. The primary endpoint — HbA1c reduction at 24 weeks — was met by 68% of the treatment arm (n=120) versus 22% in the placebo group (n=120), a statistically significant difference (p < 0.001). Mean HbA1c reduction in the treatment arm was 1.4% (±0.3). Secondary endpoints included body weight reduction (mean −4.2 kg in treatment vs −0.8 kg placebo) and fasting plasma glucose improvement. The most common adverse event was mild-to-moderate headache (12% treatment, 8% placebo). Nausea was reported in 9% of the treatment arm, primarily in weeks 1–4. No serious cardiac events, pancreatitis cases, or thyroid abnormalities were recorded during the 24-week period. A Phase III trial is planned for Q1 2026 with 1,200 participants and an 18-month follow-up.

title: Contraindications – Warfarin
content: Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant of the coumarin class used for the prevention and treatment of thromboembolic disorders. Absolute contraindications include: pregnancy (teratogenic in first trimester; risk of fetal haemorrhage in third trimester), active clinically significant bleeding disorders, haemorrhagic stroke within the past 3 months, and known hypersensitivity to Warfarin or other coumarin derivatives. Relative contraindications and high-risk situations requiring heightened caution: elderly patients (≥ 75 years) due to increased fall risk and altered pharmacokinetics; patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30) or hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B or C); recent major surgery or trauma within 72 hours; patients with poorly controlled hypertension (SBP > 180 mmHg consistently); and those with a history of gastrointestinal bleeding. Drug interactions that substantially increase bleeding risk include concurrent antiplatelet agents (Aspirin, Clopidogrel), NSAIDs, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), azole antifungals (Fluconazole), and several antibiotics. Reversal agents: Vitamin K (oral or IV) for non-urgent reversal; 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) for urgent reversal in life-threatening haemorrhage.

title: Dosage & Administration – Lisinopril
content: Lisinopril is an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor used in the management of hypertension, heart failure (HFrEF), and diabetic nephropathy. It is also indicated for haemodynamically stable patients within 24 hours of acute myocardial infarction. Mechanism of action: inhibits conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion, thereby lowering blood pressure and reducing cardiac afterload. Standard dosage for hypertension: initiate at 5–10 mg once daily, titrated every 2–4 weeks based on blood pressure response, up to a maximum of 40 mg/day. For heart failure: start at 2.5–5 mg once daily, target dose 20–35 mg/day. For diabetic nephropathy: 10–20 mg/day to reduce proteinuria and slow progression of renal disease. Dose adjustment required in renal impairment: eGFR 10–30 mL/min, start at 2.5 mg/day; eGFR < 10, use with extreme caution. Common side effects: dry persistent cough (up to 20% of patients due to bradykinin accumulation), hypotension (especially after first dose), dizziness, and hyperkalaemia. Serious but rare: angioedema (contraindicated if prior history of ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema). Contraindicated in pregnancy (all trimesters — risk of fetal renal dysgenesis and oligohydramnios) and in combination with aliskiren in patients with diabetes or renal impairment.

title: Pharmacokinetics – Atorvastatin
content: Atorvastatin (brand name Lipitor) is a synthetic HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) used for the management of hypercholesterolaemia and the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular events. Mechanism: competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, reducing LDL-C by 37–55% depending on dose. Absorption: rapidly absorbed after oral administration; peak plasma concentration (Tmax) reached in 1–2 hours. Bioavailability is approximately 14% due to extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism. Metabolism: primarily hepatic via CYP3A4; major active metabolites are ortho-hydroxy and para-hydroxy atorvastatin, which account for approximately 70% of circulating HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity. Half-life: parent drug 14 hours; active metabolites up to 20–30 hours, enabling once-daily dosing. Excretion: primarily biliary (>98%); renal clearance is negligible. No dose adjustment required for renal impairment. Dosage: 10–80 mg once daily, taken at any time of day. Drug interactions: CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, grapefruit juice) significantly increase atorvastatin plasma concentrations and myopathy risk. Avoid co-administration with fusidic acid. Ciclosporin increases atorvastatin AUC by approximately 8.7-fold; use lowest effective dose. Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis risk is elevated with fibrates (especially gemfibrozil). Monitoring: baseline LFTs before initiation; routine monitoring not required unless symptomatic.
